bill-walker-alexis-1910-07-31.A1:
WOMAN VICTIM OF BLACK FIEND Assaulted And Slashed by Negro. MOB METES QUICK JUSTICE Sheriff And Posse Hastens in Pursuit. AFTER OUTRAGING WHITE WO- MAN NEGRO VISITS HOME OF COMPANION, KILLS HIM AND STEALS WIFE.
Mobile, July 31.—(Special.)—Mrs. J. O. Gibson, a well known resident of Axis, eighteen miles north of Mobile, in this county, and on the Southern Railway, was the victim soon after 1 o'clock this morning of one of the foulest crimes in the history of this section.

She was assaulted by a negro brute, and was frightfully slashed by the fiend. Her little brother, Clarence, aged 8 years, also was slashed by the brute when he cried out for help after seeing the purpose of the fiend.

News of the terrible crime was rushed to the city to Sheriff Drago as soon as possible, and with deputies and newspaper men rushed in automobiles to the scene. Later it was learned that the rape fiend had visited the home of a negro, shot him to death and left with his victim's wife for parts unknown.

At midnight tonight word reached Mobile by telephone from Charles Anderson, at Axis, that Bill Walker, Mrs. Gibson's assailant, had undoubtedly been shot or lynched by a posse. Anderson reported that the wife of Jesse Brown, forced by Walker to accompany him after Walker had mortally wounded her husband, had returned to Axis.

She said Walker had taken her to a water tank at Cold Creek Station, three and a half miles from Axis, and when a train pulled up, Walker tried to board it. There were members of a posse aboard the train and as Walker attempted to board the train, the posse opened fire. The woman said she suddenly realized she was free and made a dash for home. She could not say what fate Walker met.

First reports from the scene of the tragedy were to the effect that William Walker, a negro, went to the Gibson home, the head of the family being absent, awoke Mrs. Gibson and told her a neighbor had just died and that he had been sent for her.

Hastily dressing and accompanied by little Clarence, the woman left her home with the man. When they had gotten away from the house and into the nearby woods, the negro turned upon Mrs. Gibson, seized her and assaulted her. During the scuffle the woman, in her desperate fight, after screaming, was cut on the throat and twice on the hands. Her wounds are not considered fatal. Little Clarence Howell also screamed for help and was rewarded by being slashed.

The woman tried to evade the cruelty of the negro and offered him money, but he declined this saying it was not what he wanted. After accomplishing his double crime, the negro said he had all he wanted and left.

Shoots Negro, Steals Wife.

Later it developed that Walker made his way to the home of Jesse Brown, another negro, about a half mile from the scene of his crime, called the man to the door and shot him to death then taking Brown's wife left for parts unknown.

Sheriff Drago, with deputies and others immediately upon reaching Axis began a search in every direction. Sheriff Drago declared he would not halt in his search until the negro was run to earth. It is said that irate citizens who have joined in the search will lynch the negro if they get him before the officers of the law do.

From the wounded woman, it was learned that after the second outrage, he demanded her money. She offered to go after it, but the cries of the lad had begun to be heard and the fiend made off. Citizens residing in the little mill camp soon rushed to the scene and armed, began a vigorous search for Walker.

Immediately after Sheriff Drago reached the scene in an auto he organized posses and a search is being conducted vigorously.

Mrs. Gibson and her little brother were brought to Mobile on the Southern train and taken at once to an infirmary and given all possible attention. Mrs. Gibson not only is suffering from the ugly wound in her throat and on her hands, but is in a state of collapse.

A late report from Axis is that a posse has the negro located in a swamp and will stand by until he is captured or killed.

Candidates Are Slow.

Huntsville, July 31—(Special)—It is just seven weeks until the municipal election and thus far there is no regularly announced candidate for Mayor or for any of the other city offices. Although the start will be late, the campaign is expected to be an interesting one and several candidates may be in the contest for Mayor. The prospective candidates apparently are waiting for each other to make the first move.

Cattle Laws Broken.

Huntsville, July 31—(Special)—J. M. Cobb, Robert Cobb and Albert Cobb, members of one family at Owens Cross Roads, were given a hearing Saturday afternoon by Commissioner Greenleaf of the United States Court on charges of interfering with the cattle quarantine officers. They were all bound over to the Federal grand jury and required to give bonds in the sum of $300 each.

Experts at Double Springs.

Double Springs, July 31. (Special.)

Congressman John L. Burnett of this district, and his corps of Agricultural Experts, and Good Roadsmen, who are making a tour of the district, lecturing on up-to-date farming stock, raising and road improvement met a large audience of farmers here yesterday. Perhaps this was the largest crowd gathered in Double Springs since the last term of circuit court. The best method of improving the soil, diversifying the crops, etc., were discussed in detail by the Government Experts.

FULL GROWN COTTON BOLL
SENT FROM MT. MEIGS

Evidently the fact that the cotton plant near Montgomery is beginning to fruit, E. L. Gilder, a farmer living near Mt. Meigs sent a full grown, open boll to The Advertiser Sunday morning The cotton was planted on March 8, according to the note which accompanied the boll. The staple is very good, and shows that the heavy rains of the early summer have not hurt that particular field.

WILL MAKE AMERICAN FAIR.

German Educators Secured to Discuss Industrial Education.

Boston, July 31.—(Special.)—The fourth annual convention of the National Society for the Promotion of Industrial Education will be held in Boston, November 17, 18 and 19. A feature of this gathering which contains especial interest is the expected presence of Dr. Georg Kerschensteiner, Superintendent of Schools, Munich, Bavaria.

Dr. Kerschensteiner will spend four weeks in America during the fall as the guest of the National Society, and will visit the schools of Boston, Chicago, St. Louis, Cincinnati and New York, at the same time delivering addresses in each of the above named cities.

The Friday evening session of the convention is to be taken up by Dr. Kerschensteiner's address on "Continuation Schools." Separate sessions will be devoted to the following topics:

"Part Time and Evening Schools,"

"Apprentice and Corporation Schools," and "The Broader Aspects of Industrial Education."
bill-walker-alexis-1910-07-31.A4:
VENGEANCE IS SWIFT
Special by United Press
Alexis, La., Aug. 1. After criminally assaulting and probably fatally stabbing Mrs. Nettie Gibson, aged 31, white, and slashing her 8-year-old brother with a razor, shooting Jess Brown and forcing the latter's wife to take to the woods with him, Bill Walker, a negro, was shot to death this morning and his body was burned by a mob.
bill-walker-alexis-1910-07-31.A21:
Hunt Negro in Swamp.
Mobile, Aug. 1—The capture of Bill Walker, the negro who early Sunday morning assaulted Mrs. J. O. Gibson, of Axis, Ala., and who later killed a negro and then stole the latter's wife, forcing her to remain with him until he was fired upon as he tried to board a Southern Railway train at Cold Creek crossing, is expected tonight or early tomorrow morning.

Sheriff Drago and three deputies put bloodhounds on the trail but the dogs after trailing for half a mile the trail suddenly went blind. After a delay of two hours, the hounds struck another trail, but the sheriff and the three deputies left for Mobile and could not say what was the result of the dogs' chase. The deputies from the jail who went after the negro reported with a rifle anfd heading or Mobile, could not find their man.

Walker this morning, at the point of a rifle, forced a negro couple to give him breakfast. The negroes knew Walker. Walker would have been captured last night were it not for the anxiety of the fireman of the train who opened fire on the negro before the posse had a chance to surround him.
bill-walker-alexis-1910-07-31.A30: ALEXIS. Ga., Aug. 1.—Bill Walker, a colored gentleman, was shot to death and his body cremated by a mob here today. Walker had assaulted and fatally wounded Nettie Gibson, the wife of a white farmer, and he was caught shortly after he had committed the crime. A crowd quickly gathered and dealt out rough justice to the coon. The authorities were powerless to prevent the lynching.
bill-walker-alexis-1910-07-31.A31:
HUSBAND IDENTIFIES GUN DECLARES NEGRO STOLE IT FROM HIS HOME. Prisoner Charged With Crime Against Woman Heavily Guarded and Special Session of Grand Jury is Requested.
Mobile, Aug. 10.—(Special.—J. O. Gibson, husband of the woman who was outraged by a negro at Axis, on the morning of July 31, called at the county jail this afternoon and identified the Winchester rifle that was found at Magazine Point yesterday, where Bill, alias Gus Walker, the negro charged with the crime and that of killing Jesse Brown, had hidden it.

This gun was stolen from the Gibson house after the negro had assaulted Mrs. Gibson and cut her son. Gibson identified the marks on the gun.

C. M. Kirk, the head of the Pennsylvania Lumber Company at Axis, called at the county jail this afternoon and identified the man as Walker. The negro denied to Kirk that he had raped Mrs. Gibson, but admitted that he killed Jesse Brown.

Charles Page, a negro whom Walker said committed the crime on Mrs. Gibson after he was locked up in jail yesterday, was brought to the county jail today and closely questioned. Page proved an alibi immediately, and was released. He stated that Walker was with him the Saturday night before the crime was committed, and had been in trouble with a negro man about cursing in the presence of his wife.

The Sheriff last night, until daylight this morning, had a double guard on duty, all armed with shot guns, and the jail was patrolled in the late hours. This guard will be kept on duty tonight. The negro will not be removed from the jail but kept there and protected.

Sheriff John S. Drago sent the following letter to Judge O. J. Semmes at Coden, his summer home:

"Hon. O. J. Semmes, Judge of the City Court of Mobile County:

"The Solicitor for Mobile County informs me that under sections of the Code of Alabama, 1907, it is within your authority to convene a special grand jury immediately to try cases where the public good demands them.

"In the case of one John Walker, now confined in Mobile County jail, I am satisfied that we have sufficient evidence to convict him of rape, also of murder in the first degree, and the people of Mobile County, as well as those in the city have freely expressed themselves that a speedy trial of Walker should be obtained, and considering their views of the matter, as well as my conclusion that an immediate trial would result in public good and satisfy the public demand, I am going to request that you convene a grand jury at your earliest moment of doing so, for the purpose of indicting Walker and placing him on trial for the alleged crime. (Signed.) "John S. Drago, "Sheriff."

bill-walker-alexis-1910-07-31.A38:
TO AN UGLY CRIME
ADMITS HE IS THE ASSAILANT OF MRS. GIBSON—IS RUSHED TO THE MOBILE JAIL TO AVOID A LYNCHING
Mobile, August 22.—(Special.)—Arthur Neill, a negro recently sent to the stockade at Vinegar Bend for vagrancy, yesterday confessed to a warden and later to Mobile deputies that he assaulted Mrs. J. O. Gibson, cut her with a knife and also slashed her young brother on the morning of July 31. The confession was carefully guarded until this afternoon when Mobile deputies, seeing a mob forming, brought the negro to this city on a through freight train. When the negro was ordered to disrobe at the stockade to put on convict stripes blood was discovered on his clothing. This he could not explain and was forced to confess.

Gus Walker some time ago was arrested at Benndale, Miss., for the crime against Mrs. Gibson. The negro was brought to Mobile and closely guarded in the county jail to prevent a lynching. Walker admitted killing a negro and stealing the latter's wife but strongly maintained his innocence of assailing Mrs. Gibson.

Two days after Walker's arrest Mrs. Gibson, accompanied by her husband, called at the Mobile jail and identified Walker as her assailant. Her identification at the time was considered positive in that she picked Walker out from a bunch of negro prisoners and pointing at the black said, "That's the man." She was positive that she was right at the time.

Citizens of Vinegar Bend upon hearing of Neill's confession were thrown into great excitement and there was strong talk of lynching.

This afternoon according to the deputies the lynching bee was so busy at Vinegar Bend the Mobile deputies had the agent flag a fast freight train, placed the negro Neill abroad and reached Mobile shortly after 6 o'clock. News of the nego's confession did not become known here until the arrival of the negro.

There is some excitement here that may become serious later tonight.
bill-walker-alexis-1910-07-31.A41:
MRS. J. O. GIBSON HEARS NEGRO TELL OF CRIME. Details of Assault at Axis Are Given at the County Jail-Previous Confession Is Repeated.
Mobile. Aug. 26—(Special.)—Mrs. J. O. Gibson, who was criminally assaulted at Axis, the later part of July, visited the county jail today and held a conversation with Arthur Neil, the negro who has confessed to committing the outrage.

Before seeing him, Deputy Sheriff Wade brought Neil to the entrance of the guard room leading from the negro portion of the jail, and there Neil repeated, so that Mrs. Gibson could hear it, the confession he had previously made to Deputy Wade.

When he was brought before Mrs. Gibson he became greatly excited, but later quieted down and answered questions she propounded to him. He named the exact amount of money he had taken from Mrs. Gibson on the night of the assault, stating that it was $8 in all, including a $5 bill. He also described to Mrs. Gibson the two gold rings and also the rifle which he took from the house. Neil has not been shown the rifle since he was placed in jail, yet his description of it was accurate.

He said he did not remember how he cut the little brother of Mrs. Gibson, but said the boy annoyed him with his attacks and he might have slashed him during the excitement without knowing it.

Mrs. Gibson stated after her talk with Neal that she could not see how it could be anybody else who attacked her as Neil knew the whole affair in every detail. She said it was a dark night and difficult to see but the voice of Neil sounded very much like that of the man who committed the crime upon her.
bill-walker-alexis-1910-07-31.A42:
GET TURPENTINE IN IMPROVED WAY
MOBILE COMPANY WILL BE FORMED TO TAKE IT FROM TREES IN AIRTIGHT BOTTLES—NEGRO WALKER ARRAIGNED
Mobile, September 5.—(Special.)—It was learned this afternoon that a Mobile lawyer is working out plans for incorporating a company to promote the Gilmer system of getting turpentine from trees in air-tight jars. G. H. Howze and T. M. McCall, two of the three men owning the new patent, admitted that within a few days the company will be organized. They would not give out any of the details of the incorporation, but stated the company would be organized upon a solid basis. Under the new system no hacking a tree, which eventually kills the timber, is necessary. A three-quarter of an inch hole is bored into the sap of the tree, and is covered with a metal cap. Attached to the cap is a three-inch metal lead and another cap, which fits over a glass jar, making an air-tight conductor for the turpentine from the time it leaves the tree until the jar is filled. The turpentine in the jar, being protected from the air, loses none of the strength by evaporation. On top of the crude turpentine in the air-tight jars can be seen pure turpentine oil, which brings $4 a
purse turpentine oil, which brings $4 a gallon on the market, and which is entirely wasted under the present box system in use by turpentine men. Experiments in distilling the turpentine collected under the new system has proved that two barrels of crude turpentine will make one barrel of turpentine. Turpentine men now figure on getting one barrel of turpentine out of every six barrels distilled.

Bill Walker, the negro who was indicted recently by a special judge on the charge of criminally assaulting Mrs. J. O. Gibson, a white woman, murdering Jesse Brown, a negro mill hand, and criminally assaulting Brown's wife, was arraigned this morning before Judge Semmes in the city court of Mobile county on the three charges. All the crimes were committed in Axis, a little mill town 18 miles from Mobile, early Sunday morning, July 31. Attorney G. T. McCorvey was appointed to represent the negro. Mr. Corvey said he would ask for a change of venue. Arguments for the change will be heard by the court Wednesday morning. The attorney gave as one of the reasons for his request that owing to the excitement in Mobile county over the crimes it would be impossible to get an unbiased jury in the county to hear the case. The jury trials on the charges were set for September 8, 9 and 10.

Isaac D. Enman, 82 years old, a member of Jones M. Withers camp No. 675, U. C. V., died this morning at the home of his niece in Mobile. Mr. Enman enlisted in the Alabama state artillery, Company A, in May, 1961, and took part in every battle from Shiloh to Spanish fort. There are but four survivors of the company in which he fought throughout the entire four years of the war.

The New Orleans, Mobile and Chicago Railroad company is receiving shipments of freight, flat and gondola cars, and will utilize them in the general movement of cotton along the road.
bill-walker-alexis-1910-07-31.A45:
NEGRO CONVICTED OF MURDER IN FIRST DEGREE. Black Man Charged With Assaults is Recommended For Death Penalty —Not Tried On Assault Charge.
Mobile, Sept. 8—(Special)—After being out fifteen minutes the jury in the case of Bill Walker, returned into court at 6:10 o'clock tonight with a verdict of guilty of murder in the first degree with recommendation that he be given the death penalty.

Before the argument to the jury, Walker was placed on the stand and admitted firing into the Brown house, but said he was desirous of killing Katie Brown as she had failed to keep an engagement with him. Judge Semmes stated after the trial that he had consulted with Solicitor Stallsworth and they decided it was not necessary to try Walker for the criminal assault on Mrs. J. O. Gibson, white, and Kate Brown, negro. Even should an appeal be taken by Walker's counsel, said Judge Semmes, the negro's own statement would be sufficient to convict him.

Walker will be brought into the city court tomorrow morning at 10 o'clock and be given the sentence recommended by the jury.

e-c-perdue-muscogee-1910-08-22.A2:
FOILS NEGROES; POSSE PURSUES Attack Made Upon Florida Woman. BOYS HEAR HER SCREAMS Assailants, Frightened, Takes to Flight. POSSE IMMEDIATELY IS ORGANIZED AND TRACES NEGRO TO SWAMPS—BRAVE GIRL DRIVES BLACKS AWAY.
Pensacola, Fla., Aug. 22—(Special)—A big posse of citizen searched the swamps this afternoon for a negro charged with having attempted to assault Mrs. Julia Middleton residing near Muscogee and who was only precented from carrying out his purpose by some small boys, whoird the screams of the woman and ran to the house.

Mrs. Middleton was alone in the house, which the negro evidently knew, and he entered through a side door. She heard a noise, according to her statement, and turned to see the negro close upon her.

Before she could move, the negro grabbed her, and placing one hand over her mouth, was struggling with her when she managed by some means to break his hold upon her and began screaming.
She screamed three or four times before the negro could again put his hand over her mouth, but the small boys heard her and ran to the house. The negro, not knowing who was coming, jumped and fled through a window.

A posse was formed immediately and the negro traced to the swamps.

Return With Negroes.

At 7:30 o'clock tonight Sheriff Van Pelt, with a force of deputies, reached the city from Muscogee, having in their custody, E. C. and John Perdue, the two negroes charged with having attempted to assault Mrs. Middleton and who two hours later went to the home of Mr. Lowery, where they found Miss Lena Lowery alone.

Their alleged attempt there was a failure as the young lady, with rare presence of mind, secured a brace of revolvers when she saw the negroes approaching, and when they came close enough and asked for some water, they found themselves fronting two big Colts' revolvers, with orders to move.

They did, but were arrested late in the afternoon at McKinnon's Creek. E. C. Perdue was wounded, when he resisted arrest. Mrs. Middleton identified both negroes.

Another negro brought in at the same time is Keyser Brown. All three are in the county jail. There is some excitement, but no serious trouble is anticipated.
e-c-perdue-muscogee-1910-08-22.A4:

Suspected of being the parties who Sunday night attempted to criminally assault Mrs. Middleton, a white lady, residing near Muscogee, and also of being the parties to go to the home of Floyd. Kittrell, some miles distant, where they were compelled to flee at the point of a revolver in the hands of Miss Lena Bowman, two negroes, both giving the name of Perdue, were brought to the city early last night and lodged in the county jail. Both were arested by Deputies Andrews and Bowman near McKinnon's creek, who accompanied Sheriff Van Pelt to the city with the prisoners. There was some excitement on the streets at the time, as the officers also brought in with them Keyser Brown, charged with murder, but the little excitement soon subsided.

CHOKED MRS. MIDDLETON.

Two negroes, it is charged, entered the home of Mrs. Middleton about 9 o'clock Sunday night and one of them grabbed her and tried to choke her down, but with his companion ran when the woman put up a plucky fight and screamed for help. Neighbors ran to aid her and spread the alarm. A search was instituted at once and late yesterday afternoon Deputy Sheriff Andrews arrested E. R. Purdue and another negro of the same name as suspects. Andrews says he carried the negroes before Mrs. Middleton, that she identified E. R. Purdue as the negro who choked her and that Purdue made a break for liberty at once. The officer clubbed the negro with his pistol, cutting his scalp so badly that it had to be sewed when he reached the jail. The other negro was so frightened that he trembled like a leaf and fell inside his cell when he reached the county jail in what is called a jail fit, but recovered afterwards.

A PLUCKY WOMAN.

Before being captured the two negroes went to the place of Floyd Kittell and attempted to come up to the house, but Miss Lena Lowry, daughter of Deputy Sheriff Lowry, grabbed a pistol and drove them away. She then notified her father of what had happened and described the negroes. Mr. Lowry joined Andrews and with him brought the negroes to jail.

Both Andrews and Lowry seemed positive that the right negroes had been captured and Andrews said there was no question as Mrs. Middleton had identified one of the negroes as her assailant.

Mrs. Middleton was not badly injured by the negro who grabbed her, as she fought him so furiously and raised such a cry that it brought help immediately.
e-c-perdue-muscogee-1910-08-22.A5:
TWO NEGROES ARE CAUGHT BY SHERIFF
Pensacola, Fla., August 22.—Charged with attempting to commit criminal assault on Mrs. Middleton, who lives in the country west of Pensacola, John and E. C. Perdue, two negroes, were caught in a swamp by a sheriff's posse late today and brought here.

According to Mrs. Middleton, some small boys prevented the negroes from carrying out their purpose. When the boys heard the screams of the woman they ran to the house to investigate and the negroes, hearing running footsteps, fled.

A few hours later the negroes went to the home of a man named Lowry, five miles distant, where they found Miss Lena Lowry, an 18-year-old girl, alone. She saw them coming and, securing a brace of pistols, she leveled them at the negroes when they were about to enter the house and ordered them to leave, which they did.
e-c-perdue-muscogee-1910-08-22.A8:
S. T. ANDREWS IS DISCHARGED BY THE SHERIFF SHERIFF LEARNED THAT THERE WAS NO TRUTH IN THE STATE- MENTS MADE BY ANDREWS RE- GARDING NEGROES—THE MEN HAD NEVER CONFESSED AND ARE NOT THE RIGHT ONES.
Deputy Sheriff S. T. Andrews, the man who arrested the two Perdue negroes and charged them with criminal assault upon Mrs. Middleton near Muscogee, was yesterday relieved of his commission by Sheriff Van Pelt, the latter writing a letter to the deputy in the morning telling him to send in his commission at once, as he is no longer in the employ of the sheriff.

This action was taken after the sheriff had learned the true state of affairs relating to the arrest of the two negroes, and the manner in which Andrews had treated them. The sheriff was angry when he learned how Andrews had acted, and said that The statements made by the deputy were a tissue of falsehoods. Instead of the two negroes being identified by Mrs. Middleton the latter very emphatically told Andrews the negroes were not the ones. In the face of this, Andrews brought the two negroes to the city, after badly beating up one of them. Upon reaching the county jail he turned to the crowd and informed them for what the negroes were arrested and added: "I'm the bully that can straddle them—they're the right negroes, boys."

CONDITION OF NEGROES.

According to the statement of the sheriff the two Perdue negroes were in no condition to leave the jail yesterday, after the rough handling Andrews gave them and the sheriff said he feared one of them might not leave the jail alive. He says that he told the negroes there was no charge against them and if they were able and wished to do so they could go there own way.

While the jailer and the chief deputy was assuring people about the jail Monday night that the negroes were not the right ones, Andrews was making his way down Palafox street talking with many people, describing their crime and assuring them that he had captured the right negroes and that they had been identified. The action of Andrews at the jail and his subsequent action was taken by many as nothing short of attempt to start a race riot.

BOILER BURSTS; TWO DIE TWO OTHERS INJURED IN SAW-MILL EXPLOSION. Sheriff And Police Chief Outwit Mob That Fails To Materialize—Negro Prisoners Removed From Jail.
Pensacola, Fla., Aug. 24—(Special)—Two were killed and two badly injured in a boiler explosion at the Nicholas saw mill at Mossy Head, a small town east of here, late yesterday afternoon, the injured being brought here for treatment today.

The dead are Engineer John Hullion and Sam Shellby, while John Hinote, one of the owners of the plant and William Marlow, the latter fireman, were badly injured.

Both ends of the boiler blew out just as the machinery had been stopped for the day, and the explosion was so great that it was heard for five miles. The plant was badly wrecked, and it was due to the fact that the mill hands had just left that more were not killed or injured.

Sheriff VanPelt and Chief Sanders, with forces of police and deputy sheriffs, formed a force of tired men this morning when they left for their homes after an all night vigil to protect the county jail. The officers kept it a secret until after the midnight hour that they expected a visit from a mob to take out the two negroes who were arrested by Deputy Andrews and placed in jail charged with criminal assault.
Shortly before midnight, after the officers had thought everything had quieted down, the sheriff received a message from a reliable party at Muscogee advising him that a mob of countrymen had formed and had started back for Pensacola. The sheriff immediately went to the jail, and, securing a closed cab, drove to a secure place and hid the two negroes. He then returned with Chief Sanders prepared to give the mob the warmest reception a mob had ever received in this city. But the mob never arrived. The members evidently backed down on the twenty mile ride, and returned to their homes.

The father of the negroes is the prosecutor, and it is alleged that Andrews beat the negroes after they had been handcuffed, and also after he had been told by the woman before whom he carried them that they were not the right parties. THE NEGRO IS CAPTURED
Found the Girl Upon Her Knees Begging for Mercy.
ST. LOUIS, Mo., Aug. 6.—Lured by a want ad in a local paper to a room in an abandoned building, Bessie Unger, 22, was barely saved from an attack by a negro here tonight. The police broke down the door leading to the place and found the girl on her knees before the black, begging or mercy.

The negro was threatening the girl with a revolver as the police broke into the room. He sprang through the door and fled down a corridor to a window, and fell a distance of 20 feet into an alley where he was forced to surrender and was taken to police headquarters. He was identified by Miss Unger.

For a time it was feared the negro would be lynched, as a great crowd gathered about the building at 12th and Olive streets in the downtown districts. Cries of "lynch him" arose, but he was spirited away.

At the police station he gave his name as James Bradford. The ad to which Miss Unger responded follows:

"Young Lady Wanted—Neat in appearance, between 20 and 25 years of age, a high school graduate, as an assistant in office, good wages to right party and permanent position."

The girl was uninjured save for serious bruises where the negro had choked her.

Was Decoyed Into Building By Bogus Advertisement.

St. Louis, Aug. 6--Miss Bessie Unger, who was decoyed to the Culver building, 306 North Twelfth Street, tonight, by a bogus advertisement for an office assistant, was rescued tonight from the clutches of the negro janitor of the building by policemen, guided to the scene by a man, whose daughter also had answered the advertisement.

A crowd shouting "lynch the brute!" gathered before the building and the police had difficulty in saving the negro from mob violence. He said he was James Bradford, 47 years old. His pockets were filled with answers to the advertisement written by young women, and he had the photographs of five white girls.

Miss Bessie Smith answered the advertisement Thursday and gave her telephone number. That night the telephone rang and her father, J. B. Smith, answered the call and became suspicious. An ambuscade was arranged for tonight and the scream of a woman led the officers to the janitor's room, where Bradford flourished a revolver and threatened death to them if they interfered. After a struggle, he was locked up.

St. Louis, Aug. 8.—Sergeant Wade Matthews, with Miss Bessie Unger of 5038 Maple avenue, this morning applied for a warrant against James Bradford, negro janitor in the Culver building, who ensnared Miss Unger to his room in the building, Twelfth and Olive street, Saturday night. She was rescued by Sergeant Matthews and Patrolmen Cormel, Steimel and Hodgens. The police assert an attempted criminal assault against Bradford and base this on the fact that the negro locked the door of the room into which he had lured Miss Unger, and that he tried to shoot Matthews when the latter forced the door. Bradford sought to escape and was knocked from a second story window by Sergeant Matthews.

Detective Cooper, a negro, identified Bradford as James Bradfield, who on July 15, 1908, was arrested on the complaint of two white women who later testified in court that he tried to drag them into a small room on Center street.

Cooper, who made the arrest, says Bradfield wore a small tin star and represented himself as a detective. Four charges were placed against him, two of disturbing the peace and two of impersonating an officer, and he was fined $50 on each count.

White persons came to his rescue and the fines were stayed.

Bradford today declared he never intended harming one of the white girls.

"Why," he said, "I have the prettiest white wife in St. Louis. I married her in Illinois."

He refused to tell where his wife was, saying they did not live together, but that she worked in private families and that they saw one another seldom.

LOUIS, Aug. 16.—A poetical billet-doux addressed to a girl who now lives in Westminster place, which the police believe was written by a negro, James Bradford, under the alias "Dr. Merrell," was found by a plumber in an abandoned stove at the Olive street address, where the girl formerly lived.

Chief of Police Young has possession of the letter and is investigating the circumstances. The girl admits she answered one of the luring advertisements to the Culver building, but denies having received the letter which the plumber says he found.

The letter was written on the stationery of the Micnold Manufacturing company, of which W. W. Culver is president. It was inclosed in an envelope which directed the postmaster to return to W. W. Culver & Son, Culver building, Twelfth and Pine streets, where Bradford was arrested last Saturday night as he was threatening Miss Bessie Unger of 5038 Maple avenue.

"I answered the advertisement inserted in the newspapers by the negro," the girl told a reporter. "When I went to the building that day and asked for 'Dr. Merrell' the negro janitor, who I now suppose was Bradford, said the doctor was stalled on a county road, his automobile having broken down. That same day he called up and told my mother the doctor was back, but I didn't go to see him."

LETTER PROBABLY COPIED

Words in the letter are missspelled, but it reads as if copied from a literary compendium. It is as follows:

My Dear Little Dreamy Angel-Eyed Girl—I take pleasure in writing you a few lines this eve, hoping they may find you well. It seems to me a year since I saw your sweet face, though it has only been a few days. What a dream wife you would be to me if you were ever beside me.

Since I saw you last I have met others, just as I have met you, with forms divine and faces fair, but none in my estimation would compare with my little girl Bonita.

Over my life your bright face casts a ray of light, the only girl in all this world who can cause my heart to beat just with pleasure in her presence, the only little woman who can rule me and not be ruled.

What other one could bring such peace and happiness to my heart and mind and fill my soul with pleasant dreams?

I love you now when your heart is young and gay. I would love you when your auburn locks are turned to gray. I hope that some day you will wander down life's path with me, hand in hand. We will smooth each other's way.

Bless your dear little heart, be true. I am very sorry you will find nothing inclosed in this but my song of love. My people are all out of town on their vacation. I am in full charge of the place all alone. I will have much to say to you when I see you again. I hope it will be very soon. I would be very much pleased if you would find time to come and see me Wednesday evening. I am so lonely. I want to talk to you and see your face and listen to the music of your sweet voice.

See if you cannot find it in your heart to come and see me. Ol just to sit by your side is Heaven to me. Bless your dear little heart, I will call you up at 6:30.

I hope you will make no other engagement for the evening.

I must now close this letter for this time and bid you goodby until I see you.

Yours with love,

DR. MERRELL.

special to The News.
special to The News.

Biloxi, Miss., Aug. 1.—Running amuck, after having desperately attacked several persons, white and black, James Ross, a negro, aged 40, was shot and instantly killed by Police Officer R. M. Randolph, about 4 o'clock yesterday afternoon. Ross resisted arrest and made several attempts to cut the officer with a knife. The coroner's jury, after hearing a number of witnesses in the case, rendered a verdict of justifiable homicide.

Ross, who was known to be a bad negro, and who was a terror among the members of his race here, started on the warpath by running Henry Prados, another negro, out of his own house. The desperado then started out Division street and cursed at Lawrence Hilderbrand, a white man, and later sent a volley of insults at some ladies who happened to be walking past him. Meanwhile Officer Randolph was approaching and Ross said: "I don't give a —— for Mun Randolph, who in the h—— is that?"

"Drop that knife and consider youreslf under arrest," said the officer. Ross made a dive and slashed at the policeman, who backed off and shot twice over the negro's head, trying thus to frighten him, but the negro had blood in his soul. He made another dangerous lunge to cut the policeman, who then shot him through the right breast. Though shot, the negro made another dive with the knife, but this time the plucky officer shot him through the head. Ross fell forward on his face dead. It is thought the negro was under the influence of liquor.

Helena, Ga., August 11.—Jim Toler, a negro, was lynched at 1 o'clock this morning at Alamo, seven miles from here by a mob of over 100 men for having entered the room of two daughters of a prominent planter of Montgomery county Tuesday night while the girls were in bed asleep.

It is stated that one of the girls was awakened by Toler when he raised the mosquito netting over the bed, and that her screams frightened him away. Search for the negro began at once and yesterday afternoon a posse of men came upon Toler working in a corn field and accused him of the crime. He confessed his guilt, and at an early hour this morning was tied to a tree and shot to death. The mob then dispersed.

Arkansas City, Aug. 20.—Sam Hill, a negro, was shot and probably fatally wounded yesterday afternoon near this city by Deputy Sheriff J. P. Findley, the officer believing that the negro was Henry Tucker, wanted on a charge of criminal assault and the murder of a little fourteen-year-old white girl, the daughter of William Brock of this county.

Yesterday morning word came to the office of the sheriff that Henry Tucker, for whom the officers have been searching for three weeks, was to be found at a certain house in the country. Deputy Sheriff J. P. Findley went after him.

The assault on the little girl and her subsequent murder was a most horrible affair and the officer felt that should the negro learn that he was after him there would be trouble. Arriving near the house where the negro was supposed to be the deputy dismounted and slipped up to the house through the timber. The negro was sitting on a porch, and when Mr. Findley was close to him the officer dashed at him with his weapon ready to fire, calling on him with his weapon
run for a weapon in the house, and he shot to stop him.
The wounded negro was found to be one wanted by the officers, however, the grand jury in this county having recently indicted him upon a charge of grand larceny. He has also served a term in the Arkansas penitentiary from this county.
This morning the negro is not dead, but his condition is serious, and it is believed that he cannot live. No censure attaches to the action of the deputy sheriff in firing on the negro.

Cotton Seed Oil Men Rejoice.

Washington, Aug. 20.—Efforts of Edwin V. Morgan, American Minister to Uraguay, to induce that government not to increase the duty on cotton seed oil has met with some encouragement, according to a dispatch received today at the State Department from Montevideo. The Minister stated that the duty would not be increased until after the fullest consideration by the Uruguayan Congress had been made. He suggested that the American cotton seed industry make representations to the Chamber of Commerce at Montevideo.

Cotton Mills Shut Down.

Methuen, Mass., Aug. 20.—The Methuen cotton mills were closed today and will re-open September 12. About 600 hands are employed.
